item.title: Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64
item.description:
Source: calif.io

Top Comment:

From the section on performing heap grooming over the network ("Remote Heap Feng Shui"):

> The current attack is sensitive to network conditions, like RTT and jitter. Low, stable round-trip times are preferred for a more reliable attack. In our controlled environment, we performed this attack over the internet through public IP addresses instead of just assuming perfect laboratory conditions. For the current attack path to achieve optimal stability and reliability in exploitation, Calif turned to physics and utilized money to solve the problem, rather than experimenting with TCP/IP stack configuration. In other words, Calif rented another VM in the same region as our target.

And the "Limitations" section:

> There is no universal payload. Each chain needs a decoder route, a live writer, a returned reader or another feedback path, a heap layout, and an application action. Every target needs a bespoke profile. The exploit is not a universal point-and-shoot.

Based on the complexity and constraints, short-term mass-exploitation seems unlikely. It will take some time before there are reliable exploits, and they may require running on infra close to the target.

But a long tail of unpatched java applications/services at high-value targets getting exploited, seems plausible to me.

item.title: Inside Deutsche Bank
item.description:
Source: www.inside-db.com

Top Comment:

I was involved with this project as a reporter, though others from my organisation did most of the work.

HN readers may be interested to know a bit about the tech stack. The 15 million or so documents, mostly Outlook mailbox exports, were provided to partners in the consortium via a tool called OpenAleph [1], which is maintained by DARC and based on ElasticSearch and a schema called FollowTheMoney [2], developed specifically for the investigative journalism use case. A lot of the original work on this was done by Friedrich Lindenberg (@pudo), who now runs OpenSanctions [3].

The timing was v. interesting given where we are with LLMs -- it's the first major leak I've worked on where it was possible to leverage local models to do some of the heavy lifting, and this only got more possible as the project went on. The coordinators provided a centrally hosted chatbot with RAG, but I also managed to get some surprisingly useful material using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on my 24GB M2 MBA via a custom agent harness for Aleph/OpenAleph. [4]

Happy to answer any questions about techy stuff, though I'm not a spokesperson for the project by any means. Seen a few people saying "just release the data!", but I think that slightly misunderstands what this work is. The whole point of forming a consortium of hundreds of journalists and sifting through the dump is to identify the bits that are in the public interest to report on -- especially important in jurisdictions like the UK, where I'm based, which have very strong defamation laws. Think Panama Papers, not Wikileaks.

[1] https://darc.li/openaleph/ [2] https://followthemoney.tech/ [3] https://www.opensanctions.org/ [4] https://github.com/data-desk-eco/sift

item.title: Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long?
item.description:
Source: kernel.dev

Top Comment:

It's pretty obvious that Gemini 4 Carbon is not token efficient. It also has relatively low tokens-per-second compared to other models. I can think of several reasons why this is the case:

1. Google has huge amounts of cash and compute. Their goal was to train a model that that has the highest quality & frontier performance, not create a model that's efficient to run and serve. They have other models for that, like Hydrogen.

2. Google created Carbon without caring for inference costs. DeepMind is subsidized by the rest of Google's empire. Selling inference is an insignificant part of Google's revenue. But for Anthropic and OpenAI, selling inference is their entire business model. Anthropic and OpenAI have enormous incentive to sell as much inference as they can in the most efficient manner. Google doesn't have this incentive.

3. They are one of the few companies that can be inefficient. Out of all the frontier labs, Google DeepMind is probably the least constrained by compute. Chinese labs have around 10 to 100 times less compute, so they must release highly optimized models.

item.title: Multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion
item.description:
Source: www.ruby-lang.org

Top Comment:

There's what I think is probably an awesome bug here.

Windows-1252 encoding has a representation for lowercase German sharp 's' (ß), but not one for the uppercase. If you upcase a string containing a sharp 's', it gets normalized to "SS", which increases the length of the string by one character. The 1252 case conversion code doesn't handle this; it looks like it checks for headroom in the buffer one character at a time. So if the last character of a string you upcase is ß, it looks like you get a one-byte overflow (of 'S').

If that's really the bug (there's a claimed RCE POC), the heap grooming for it must be really fussy! I couldn't find any other character pairs that expand like this.

You can feed strings in 1252 to a Rails program through multipart POSTs, which get to pick their encodings.

The great thing about this bug, apart from how it illustrates how doomed we all are (if I'm right), is that it should by rights have the best vulnerability name of the year, because you get to work 'ß' into it.
